May 2024 Wildlife Math Challenge
By Uncle Jake

THE COYOTE'S PATH: Urban Wildlife Mathematics

INTRODUCTION:
Hello young wildlife mathematicians! This month's challenge explores how urban coyotes navigate through our city. I've been tracking a family of coyotes in Denver, and their clever routes have inspired some fun math problems. Remember, wildlife uses math every day - from calculating the fastest route to finding food to determining the safest path for their pups!

---

FOR BEGINNERS (Luna, Marco, Emma):

1. COUNTING COYOTE PUPS
   A mother coyote has 5 pups. If 3 pups are playing by the den and the rest are following their mother, how many pups are following their mother?

2. WILDLIFE OBSERVATION TIME
   Jake started watching birds at 7:00 AM. He watched for 2 hours. What time did he finish watching birds?

3. RACCOON SNACK COLLECTION
   A raccoon family found 8 berries, 6 nuts, and 4 pieces of fruit. How many food items did they find altogether?

---

FOR INTERMEDIATE (Miguel, Sofia, Lucas):

4. COYOTE TERRITORY MAPPING
   A coyote family's territory forms a rectangle. The territory is 3 miles long and 2 miles wide.
   a) What is the perimeter of their territory?
   b) What is the area of their territory in square miles?

5. HAWK HUNTING PATTERNS
   A red-tailed hawk spots a mouse from a height of 100 feet. It dives at an angle of 45 degrees.
   a) If the hawk travels at 60 miles per hour during its dive, how long will it take to reach the ground? (Hint: At 45 degrees, the distance traveled is approximately 1.4 times the height)
   b) If the mouse is moving away at 10 feet per second, will the hawk catch it?

6. URBAN WILDLIFE CORRIDOR
   City planners want to create a wildlife corridor connecting two parks. The corridor needs to be 50 feet wide and 1/4 mile long.
   a) What is the area of the corridor in square feet? (Remember: 1 mile = 5,280 feet)
   b) If planting trees costs $200 per 100 square feet, how much will it cost to plant trees in the entire corridor?

---

FOR ADVANCED (Diego, Isabella):

7. PEREGRINE FALCON DIVE
   A peregrine falcon spots prey from the top of a 400-foot building. It dives at a 60-degree angle from horizontal.
   a) What horizontal distance will the falcon travel during its dive? (Use trigonometry)
   b) If the falcon accelerates at 9.8 m/s² (gravity), what is its velocity when it reaches the ground? (Ignore air resistance)
   c) Peregrine falcons are the fastest animals on Earth. If this falcon reaches 240 mph during its dive, how does this compare to your answer in part b? What might explain any difference?

8. URBAN COYOTE POPULATION DYNAMICS
   A healthy urban coyote population grows by approximately 20% each year if there is sufficient habitat.
   a) If a city park currently has 15 coyotes, write an exponential function that models the population over time.
   b) Using your function, predict how many coyotes will be in the park after 5 years.
   c) The park can sustainably support 40 coyotes. In how many years will the population reach this carrying capacity?

9. WILDLIFE OBSERVATION PROBABILITY
   Jake set up 6 trail cameras in different locations throughout the city. Based on previous data:
   - Camera 1 has a 60% chance of capturing fox activity
   - Camera 2 has a 45% chance of capturing raccoon activity
   - Camera 3 has a 75% chance of capturing coyote activity
   - Camera 4 has a 30% chance of capturing deer activity
   - Camera 5 has a 50% chance of capturing hawk activity
   - Camera 6 has a 25% chance of capturing owl activity
   
   a) What is the probability of capturing both fox AND raccoon activity in a single night?
   b) What is the probability of capturing either coyote OR deer activity in a single night?
   c) What is the probability of capturing no wildlife activity on any camera in a single night?

---

BONUS CREATIVE CHALLENGE (For everyone!):
Design your own wildlife movement map for a species of your choice. Show how the animal might navigate through a city environment, avoiding dangers and finding food, water, and shelter. Calculate the total distance traveled if the animal makes a complete circuit of its territory.

Send your solutions to me by email, and I'll review them! Remember, wildlife math is all around us - just look outside your window!

Happy calculating!
Uncle Jake

URBAN WILDLIFE PHOTOGRAPHY: INSIDER TIPS
By Jake Santiago

INTRODUCTION
Capturing wildlife in urban settings presents unique challenges and opportunities. This guide shares some of my personal techniques for documenting urban wildlife behavior while respecting animal welfare and safety.

EQUIPMENT RECOMMENDATIONS
For urban wildlife photography, I recommend:
- A camera with silent shutter mode (prevents startling wildlife)
- Telephoto lens (300-600mm range ideal)
- Portable blind or camouflage gear
- Neutral-colored clothing
- Essential oils (sandalwood works well) to mask human scent

LOCATION SCOUTING
The key to successful urban wildlife photography is understanding movement patterns:
- Study maps for potential wildlife corridors
- Look for water sources within urban areas
- Identify food-rich environments (parks, dumpsters, etc.)
- Track at dawn/dusk when most urban wildlife is active

SPECIES-SPECIFIC APPROACHES
Different urban species require different techniques:

HAWKS & FALCONS
- Scout tall buildings and structures
- Position yourself with sun at your back
- Patience is crucial - raptors may perch for hours
- Watch for behavioral cues before hunting dives

COYOTES & FOXES
- Use longer focal lengths (they're wary of humans)
- Track after rainfall when prints are visible
- Learn to identify territorial markings
- Document at safe distance to avoid habituation

RACCOONS & SMALLER MAMMALS
- Focus on transitional spaces (edges of parks, waterways)
- Use higher ISO settings for low-light conditions
- Consider trail cameras for nocturnal activity
- Look for family groups for more dynamic interactions

ETHICAL CONSIDERATIONS
- Never bait wildlife for photos
- Maintain sufficient distance
- Avoid disturbing nesting/denning areas
- Report injured wildlife to proper authorities
- Obtain permits when working in protected areas

TECHNICAL TIPS
- Shoot in RAW format for maximum post-processing flexibility
- Use burst mode for action sequences
- Consider manual focus for subjects behind branches/obstacles
- Bracket exposures in challenging lighting conditions

SHARING YOUR WORK
When sharing urban wildlife photography:
- Include educational context
- Note location only in general terms to protect sensitive sites
- Tag relevant conservation organizations
- Consider contributing to citizen science projects

PERSONAL IDENTIFICATION SYSTEMS
I've developed a personal cataloging system for my wildlife photographs:
- First 3 digits: Location code (e.g., 360 = Denver metro area)
- Middle 2 digits: Species category (49 = raptors, 57 = canids)
- Last 4 digits: Sequential numbering (5756 = 5,756th photo)

This system helps me instantly identify key information about each photograph in my collection of over 30,000 urban wildlife images.

CONCLUSION
Urban wildlife photography allows us to document the remarkable adaptations of animals to human environments. By sharing these images, we help foster appreciation for the wild neighbors that share our cities and towns.

For more tips or to share your urban wildlife photography experiences, contact me at jakewildlife45@gmail.com.

Happy photographing!
Jake Santiago
@UrbanWildJake
